translations.text: A discourse delivered by Saint Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria, on the saying written in the Gospel according to Matthew: “The kingdom of heaven is like a rich man,
who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.”
The Lord said in the Gospel of Matthew, “The kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.
He agreed with the workers on a stater a day and sent them to his vineyards.
He went out at the third hour and saw others standing idle in the marketplace.
He said to the others, ‘You too go to my vineyard, and I will give you what you deserve.’
And they went.
He went out again at the sixth hour and the ninth hour and did the same.
When he went out again at the eleventh hour, he saw others standing there.
He said to them, ‘Why have you been standing here idle all day?’
They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’
He said to them, ‘You too go to my vineyard.’”
Let us now examine this and understand who these workers are, what this vineyard is, and who this landowner is.
First, the owner of the vineyard is God the Father, who has governed his creatures from the beginning.
Speaking with them also through the prophet, he tells us, “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is the beloved’s young planting.”
The workers whom he hired first are Moses, Aaron, and Joshua son of Nun.
He called Moses in the land of Midian, saying, “Come, go down to Egypt and bring my people out of that place.
Work in my vineyard through the commandments, the ordinances, and the decrees.”
He agreed with them on a stater: the honor of being a prophet; for Aaron, in turn, the high priesthood over his people. And they went.
Those of the third hour are the judges. He sent them too over his people: “I will give you what you deserve.”
They are not prophets, nor are they apostles. Rather, what they deserved was this title: “judges.”
Those of the sixth hour and those of the ninth hour are Samuel, David, and all the prophets.
Samuel worked in the vineyard with a horn.
David brought a vine out of the land of Egypt. He worked on it with a harp.
Hosea found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. Amos
He said, “Israel is a fine, spreading vine, and its fruit is plentiful.”
Those of the eleventh hour are the apostles, whom he found standing idle all day.
These are the ones who are idle as far as all lawless deeds are concerned, whom no one hired. The devil could not hire them to worship idols.
He could not hire John the Baptist for taverns, places for eating and drinking.
As for Peter, he could not hire him for unbelief.
As for Andrew, he could not hire him into a defiled marriage, making him a woman's slave.
For this reason he was called Boanerges, which means “the son of the thunder of heaven.”
For no one on earth could hire them to work for him and pay them according to their worth.
For their wages will be great in heaven.
For this reason the Savior said concerning all the apostles, “My Father, the people you gave me out of the world—I found them to be chosen vessels.”
Again, “Of all those you gave me, I have not lost a single one. And no one can come to me unless my Father, who sent me, draws him.”
Look, these words teach us that it is the Father who hires workers for his vineyard.
Who, then, is this manager?
I say that it is the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who holds all the Father's possessions—that is, the mysteries.
Just as his mighty works are present in Israel and among the other nations. For he himself said, “The Father loves the Son and has placed everything in his hands.”
He is a son because the inheritance belongs to him.
He is a manager because he is the one who pays the workers, and the whole world is under his authority.
For he holds the keys of David. He is a vine.
For he is the one who gladdens all creation.
He is also bread.
For he is the one who gives all creation drink.
When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his manager, “Call the workers and give them their wages.”
“Begin with the last until you reach the first, and give each one a stater.”
The Father said to the Son, “Whether at the end or during the day, you are the one who knows. Call the workers,”
“and give them their wages—all the workers who labored on behalf of the human race. Give them the wages for their work.”
Paul said, “God appointed some in the church: first, the apostles,” whom he began paying first; second, the prophets, and the rest.
The first came, thinking that they would receive more.
Listen to him. He said, “I tell you that many prophets and kings wanted to see what you see, but did not see it.”
The stater that he gave them is apostleship and the holy offering.
He said, “When they received it, they grumbled against the owner of the vineyard, saying, ‘Why?
These last workers worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us.’
Who were those who grumbled out of envy toward these last workers, other than the scribes and the Pharisees? For they too were sent to work in the vineyard.
These are the ones he cries out against: “Why have you burned my vineyard? And what you have plundered from the poor is in your house!”
For they too received the law through the commands of angels, but did not keep it. And they were grumbling against the Lord
about John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees: “They fast, but yours do not fast.”
“Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders?
They do not wash their hands when they are going to eat their bread. They eat, drink, and live indulgently.”
The apostles, for their part, rub grain and eat because they are hungry. They wander through the world.
These people also grumble, saying, “Why do your disciples break the Sabbath?” They envied these last workers, the true ones.
He answered and said to one of them, “Friend, I am not treating you unjustly.
Did I not agree with you on a stater? Take what is yours and go.”
Who was it who received all these rebukes?
I say that it was no one other than the one who was told, “Friend, do what you came to do”—that is, Judas, who assailed the Savior with loud complaints:
“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred staters and the money given to the poor?”
If you care about the poor, you traitor, why do you steal their belongings from your money box?
“Or are you envious because I am good?”
For he was wicked, stealing what was put into it,
while the Savior was good to him and patient with him.
But he said to him, “Am I not allowed to do what I want with what belongs to me?”
This is God’s defense against him: “Am I, God, not allowed to give greater wages to whoever works, and to judge those who act wickedly?”
These are the testimonies, or the complaints, of Judas. For he grumbled with his tongue,
but in his heart he was a merciless [?].
He is wicked in his soul, a thief with his hands, and shameless in his eyes.
Whenever they ate, the apostles would take care not to put their hands into the bowl before the Savior. They were afraid and said, “Who are we to eat with God?”
But Judas, the insensitive man, would plunge his hand into the bowl with the Savior,
eager to dip his piece of bread at the same time during the meal, ahead of the Savior, while the Savior would say nothing. But so that we might understand,
when the disciples asked him, “Who, then, is going to betray you?”
he gave them a sign of Judas’s insensitivity: “The one who puts his hand into the bowl with me first is the one who will betray me.”
He said to him, “Do what you are going to do quickly.”
For the Savior was eager to accomplish the salvation of his creation on the cross, according to his Father’s will and command.
For would you find him hanging back, or neglecting what he had come for, or afraid of death?
Instead, he showed his eagerness for the cross as a mighty martyr and as a fearless God.
That is why he urged Judas, “Do what you are going to do quickly.
Hurry! Come now, all created beings are waiting in suspense. They are waiting for you, and they are also waiting for me.
Those in heaven are waiting for me. Those in the abyss and chaos are waiting for you.
My Father is with me, helping me. The devil is with you. He stands with you at your right hand, helping you.
The holy angels are decorating the gates of heaven with wreaths for me. The powers of punishment are preparing the gates of Hades for you.”
He urged him with these words: “Hurry, for I am ready for the lashes.”
It is therefore rightly said to Ezra, “Creation is not in a greater hurry than the Creator.”
But if Judas was the one who would betray him, why did he address him by saying, “Friend, I am not wronging you”?
Because he had said to him, “Your eye is evil, but I am good.”
The Savior did not withdraw the name of friendship from him, even up to the moment when he betrayed him.
He called him “friend,” but Judas was thinking of hostility.
He gave him the money box, and he became a thief.
He chose him as a disciple, but Judas was plotting deceit. He chose him as a human being, and he became a devil.
O Judas, what have you done? What have you gained by betraying the Lord?
You have forfeited your life and lost this great honor—the glory of being an apostle.
For who is above their rank? After those called angels come the apostles.
For someone will scarcely consider his son worthy to eat with him, and it is impossible for a slave to eat with his master.
But Jesus our Lord considered them worthy: he ate with tax collectors and drank with Judas the lawless one. A wicked man stretched out his hand alongside God.
This wretched man ruined his own life, for he brought death upon himself. He had been raised higher than he deserved; he fell down to the ground as he deserved.
He was chosen among the apostles, but he forfeited his apostleship.
He was appointed an heir, but he alienated himself from the inheritance.
The apostles are the Savior's heirs. They are the light of the world, yet they could not give light to Judas.
They are the salt of the earth, yet they could not stop Judas's decay.
They are the ones God placed in the church, yet they could not make him remain with them.
For they had surpassed the bounds of human nature, while he came to belong to the devil.
Woe to you, Judas! What have you gained? Cain, who killed a human being, was better than Judas, who killed God.
Saul, who hated a human being, was better than Judas, who hated God.
Pharaoh's hardheartedness toward the people was better than Judas's hardheartedness toward God.
Balaam's error was better than Judas's lawlessness.
Korah's rebellion in the wilderness was better than Judas's stubbornness in Jerusalem.
Achan, who hid things devoted to destruction, was better than Judas, who stole alms.
Absalom's arrogance toward David was better than Judas's insolence toward God.
Ahithophel's evil plotting against David—he hanged himself and died—was better than Judas's accusations against the Savior: he hanged himself and ended up in Tartarus.
Shimei's curses against David were better than Judas's mockery of the Savior.
The blood Joab shed in wickedness counts for less than the blood Judas shed without mercy.
Gehazi's greed, though he became leprous, was better than Judas's greed.
He went to destruction. Jeroboam's sin is less than Judas's lawlessness. Jeroboam made a false god, while Judas cast out the true God.
Friend, I am not wronging you. Take what is yours and go.
Wicked friend, Judas, it was not the Savior who wronged you, but you yourself alone. Take the curse and go away to the underworld.
Judas ended up in these circumstances. Matthias came in and received the blessing. He became a disciple at the Teacher's feet.
He became an apostle and preached.
He became a light to the regions.
He became salt and seasoned souls. He became a servant and submitted to the Lord.
He became a son of God's beloved, Jesus Christ, the king of all.
The Lord of all, the glory of all, the one who governs all, the one who will judge all, the one who had compassion on all,
the one who is merciful to all, the one who died for all, the one who rose for all, the one who set all free, the one who transformed all,
the one who made all things new, the one who made all rejoice, the one through whom all flourishes.
Now then, come, you mortal, and board the ship of salvation, which is the faith of the church.
It has two oars that propel it. These are the two Testaments, which you study. They will bring you to the good anchorage.
It has a mast and a yard, which are the Lord's cross. These are your two hands, stretched out in prayer to God.
It has a sail that draws it along. This is the Lord's authority, which will guide you along every good path.
It has a helmsman, who is the bishop in the church.
The captain is in command. This is Jesus, who governs all.
It has sailors aboard. These are the clergy who serve in the church.
Passengers have boarded it. These are the Christian people.
And you will dock in the good harbor, which is the haven of Jesus, the heavenly Jerusalem.
And you will inherit God's promises, which are his good gifts, and rest with your fellow citizens, who are the angels and all the saints.
Now then, brothers and sisters, look: we have spent the whole day exercising ourselves in the word, until we completed the task we undertook.
Now then, let us give thanks to God and the Holy Spirit,
who opened the door of the Word for us and put speech in our mouths, so that we could speak the things the Word graciously granted us for the benefit of our souls and those who listen to us.
And let us bless the Word, who graciously gave us the Holy Spirit.
For he himself also said, "When they speak with you, do not worry about what you will say, for what you are to say will be given to you at that very hour.
For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks within you."
Let us, for our part, give glory to God, to God the Almighty, who sent us the king, Christ,
through whom we bless and sing praises to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Trinity of one substance, from eternity through all eternity. Amen.
Athanasius, Archbishop.
Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria, speaking about mercy and justice.
My brothers, the world that forgets God is held captive by the oppression inflicted on its neighbors and by the cruelty inflicted on the powerless.
As the holy apostle says, “Just as they did not see fit to keep God before them in uprightness, God handed them over to a worthless mind, to do what is improper,
filled with every kind of injustice, malice, wickedness, and greed, full of envy and murder,
strife, deceit, and an evil heart; whisperers, slanderers, haters of God, insolent people,
arrogant people, boasters, people who seek out evil,
who do not obey their parents, senseless, unfaithful, hardhearted, unfaithful, hardhearted, merciless.”
Those whom God turns toward worshiping him, he also teaches to keep away from evil and to exercise spiritual concern for their neighbors.
As Isaiah taught us, speaking on God's behalf: “Stop your wickedness; learn to do good.”
For the law contains many commands not to harm our neighbor. It also contains commandments about kindness toward others and showing mercy to one another.
For if someone neglects one of these, the other is not enough to keep that person standing.
For someone who does good to the needy with profits gained through oppression is not acceptable before God either.
But if he is not going to give anything from what he has—for concerning those who commit injustice and attempt to offer a gift to God,
it is written, “The sacrifice of the ungodly is an abomination to the Lord.”
As for the person who is stingy, he says about him, “Whoever closes his ears so as not to hear a poor person will himself call upon God, and God will not listen to him.”
For this reason Proverbs advises us, “Honor God with the proceeds of your honest labor, and give him the firstfruits from the fruits of your righteousness.”
For if you are going to bring a gift to God from oppression and robbery,
it is far better neither to acquire such property for yourself nor to offer a gift from it.
For you must bring what you have vowed as a holy gift, as it is written, “The vows of the upright are acceptable to him.”
Again, if you acquire possessions through honest labor but do not bring offerings to God from which the poor are supported, they will be counted against you as robbery.
As he says through the prophet Malachi, “The firstfruits and tithes are [?] you, and robbery will be in your houses.”
For now we must combine mercy with justice: we must acquire with justice and distribute with mercy, according to what is written:
“Keep mercy and justice, and draw near to your God at all times.”
For God loves mercy and justice, so that whoever takes care to show mercy may be pleasing to the Lord.
So now, at this point, let each person examine himself.
Let the rich person examine the things he acquires, from which he intends to make gifts to God: has he oppressed the poor?
Has he used force against the weak? Has he exploited someone beneath him, using authority instead of justice?
For we are commanded to maintain justice and fairness toward our fellow servants.
Do not oppress others because you have authority, or exploit them because you have power.
Instead, because you have the means to exercise authority, display deeds of justice.
For through something you are unable to do,
how will you demonstrate your restraint and your fear of God? Rather, it is through something in which you can transgress but do not transgress.
But if you take the possessions of the poor and give them to other poor people, you would do better neither to plunder nor to give.
Why do you defile your wealth by adding unjust deeds to it?
Why do you make your offering an abomination, attempting to offer it through oppression, while thinking that by it you are showing mercy to other poor people?
Have mercy on the person you are oppressing.
Show kindness to that person, and be generous to this one.
Then you will fulfill both mercy and justice.
For does God share in greed? Nor is God a partner in the profits of robbers. Nor has he left the poor to us because he is unable to feed them.
Rather, he seeks a just and humane offering from us, for our freedom and for our benefit.
Can mercy come from oppression, or blessing from a curse, or kindness from tears?
For God, moved by the tears of those who are oppressed, says, “These are the things I hate, which you are doing:
you cover my altar with tears, with weeping, and with groaning caused by suffering.”
Deeds of this kind are acts of vanity.
They are acts of vanity.
They are done for honor from people.
They are not done for honor from God.
Therefore the Lord rightly said, “Do not act so that people will see you.”
But if you perform your act of mercy knowing that God is aware of it, you will be all the more careful not to do it out of greed,
knowing that you do not please God in this way—God, who watches over us.
Let us show mercy in such a way that we will receive its reward from God.
But God gives his good things to those whom he honors.
He does not honor anyone who is greedy.
It does you no good to offer a gift to God if you cause your brother grief.
He said, “If you come to offer a gift on the altar and remember there that your brother has something against you,
go first and make peace with your brother. Then come and offer your gift.”
Remember, then, Zacchaeus the tax collector, who resolved to repay four times as much to anyone he had defrauded.
In this way he distributed his possessions among the poor.
For he knew that he wanted to receive Christ and to have Christ receive him—not like those who lend at interest to the poor,
unless they undo their greed by making restitution for what they took by force.
And so the Lord accepted him because of Zacchaeus’s uprightness.
And he said, “Salvation has come to this house today.”
We have said these things to those who practice mercy but do not concern themselves with fairness and justice.
But we will [?] also speak to the person who takes care to avoid injustice but neglects mercy: “A fruitless tree is cut down and thrown into the fire.”
And will a tree of this kind ever please the heavenly farmer, who says, “I came looking for fruit on this fig tree and found none”?
He ordered it to be cut down so that it would not waste the soil as well.
The person who has not given the poor their share is also blamed, and a threat is made against someone like this.
He said, “Whoever neglects to give the pitiable poor person his share will cry out to God, and he will not listen to him.”
God said, “For I am merciful.”
For it is a fearful thing and contrary to the law to go back and glean your harvest,
and to go back and strip your vineyard again, and to shake your olive grove again, because these things should be left for the poor.
But if these commands were given to those under the law, what shall we say about those who are in Christ?
These are the people to whom the Lord says, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, [?] you will enter the kingdom of heaven.”
Therefore, not only from the fields and from what comes to us from outside, but also from the work of our hands,
the apostle teaches us to give to those who have nothing.
He said, “With your hands [?] good things, so that you may find a way to give to the person in need.”
But the person who wants to follow the Savior, the Lord declared blessed, so that he would give away all his remaining property for the benefit of the poor and in this way follow him.
But those who followed him, together with the perfect, having brought their abundant zeal and perfect acts of mercy to completion—
he commands them to complete their service through material possessions and move on to service through the word and the Spirit.
As for the rest, he commands them to keep giving and sharing from what they possess,
so that through these things they may find themselves imitating God's love for humanity, showing mercy, giving, and giving freely.
For he said, “Give, and you will be given to. Be kind, and kindness will be shown to you.”
Through these things, too, he promised them fellowship with him.
For these are the ones who stand at the Lord's right hand,
those to whom the King will say when he comes, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you since the foundation of the world.
For I was hungry, and you fed me.
I was thirsty, and you gave me something to drink.
I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.
I was naked, and you clothed me.
I was sick, and you visited me.
I was in prison, and you came to me.”
When the righteous are amazed and say, “Lord, when did we do these things for you?”
he will say to them, “Truly I tell you, insofar as you did it for one of these little, insignificant ones, it was for me that you did it.”
For zeal toward the saints is devotion toward Christ.
And the person who is eager to serve those who belong to Christ is found to be a servant of Christ.
Not only when he has a great deal, but even if what he has is little, let him offer it.
And if he gives a disciple just a cup of cold water to drink because he is a disciple, truly I tell you, his reward will not be lost.
He gives you, rich person, an opportunity for true freedom.
For through these things you will be found to be God's fellow worker, supporting Christ's soldiers—and supporting them willingly, without anyone forcing you.
The King of heaven does not compel anyone or collect taxes. Rather, he welcomes eager givers, so that by giving they may receive, and by showing honor they may be honored.
And they share with the poor in [?], so that they may be invited into eternal fellowship.
Let us remember these things forever, at all times.
Let them remain before our eyes and in our souls, so that when we reach the appointed time, we will not let it pass us by or forget what is happening.
Now let us look ahead to what is coming, lest our end overtake us while we are waiting and putting the work off.
May the Lord grant that we be found watchful and bearing fruit, remembering his commandments, prepared for his glorious rest, and with no one bringing any accusation against us,
through Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom glory belongs to the Father, together with him and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
Athanasius, Archbishop.
A discourse delivered by the holy patriarch Apa Athanasius, archbishop of Alexandria, concerning the soul and the body.
The word that is sent in the heavens contains no envy. It is ready to strengthen your souls.
You too must be ready to receive the power of the word. But there is also a need for someone who listens.
For just as the rain from heaven does not bear fruit without the earth, neither does the earth produce without the rain from heaven.
In the same way, the listener gains no benefit without the one who teaches him, nor does the teacher gain any without the one who listens to him.
The Word will provide the message, and let those who listen carry out their obedience fully.
For look, the Word gives his power. You too must be without envy, having first purified yourselves of every deceit, envy, and unbelief, because these are enemies of righteousness.
For jealousy opposes love, and unbelief opposes faith, just as bitterness opposes sweetness.
Darkness opposes light, evil opposes good, death opposes life, and falsehood opposes truth.
Those who are perfected in the power of the adversary are those who possess jealousy and envy,
along with unbelief, hating love and faith. Those who hate these are enemies of God.
For we know, my beloved, that everyone who is full of jealousy, envy, and unbelief is an enemy of righteousness. So guard yourselves against those who are enemies of righteousness.
Clothe yourselves in faith and love, because through these all the saints have been saved, from the beginning until now.
Therefore show the power of love, not in words alone, but in action. For the Lord gave himself as a ransom for us all.
For we did not come into being in the same way that the whole world came into being through a spoken word. Rather, he created us through both word and action.
God was not content to say, “Let us create a human being according to our likeness and our image.” Rather, he makes the action follow the word.
For God took some earth from the ground and formed it into a human being according to his image and likeness. He breathed a breath of life into his face.
But Adam came under the power of death because of his transgression. Adam, the creature God had formed, needed to be formed again by God the Creator so that he might be saved.
For the human being [?] and was buried in the earth, after the spirit had separated from him—the spirit that he had breathed into him and that had become a breath of life.
He was then held in a dark place after he died, in the place called Hades.
For the soul and the body were divided, and death separated them from one another.
The soul was bound in Hades, while the flesh, for its part, decomposed in the earth.
And there was a great distance between them—the flesh and the soul.
The flesh decayed and was scattered in the earth in which it had been buried, while the soul, for its part, became powerless in the bonds of Hades.
The strong soul was bound in darkness.
The weak one, the body, for its part, decomposed in the earth.
For the body cannot move while it lies decomposed in the mountain, nor can the soul do anything while it is bound in Hades.
For when death took the human being, it bound the strong part—that is, the soul—in Hades, while it dissolved the weak part—that is, the flesh—in the earth.
For it is like a tyrant who is going to capture a royal city: he first seizes the king and holds him securely in his power.
This is how death first attacks the soul, while the body becomes like a ship with no pilot aboard.
This is how the body perished and fell apart limb by limb, because the soul had stopped steering it.
And the limbs were scattered in the mountain. They perished like a deserted city, like a ship with no pilot aboard that has sunk into the water.
For the soul steers its own body like a king administering his city.
For when the human being died, his soul could not steer his flesh, because it was bound in Hades.
And it lost its way on the paths of righteousness, like a pilot whose ship has lost its way at sea.
The soul turned aside from the straight paths, being led astray onto the paths of robbers so that they could plunder it there.
These are adultery, sexual immorality, love of adornment, idolatry, murder, and hatred.
For these are the things through which the soul ruined the human being.
And because of these things he became a corpse in the mountains. The soul was handed over by the evil one whom it had followed, to be held captive in Hades.
For he plundered it like a robber.
But he left it to itself, unable to help its own body, which had perished.
The flesh decomposed in the earth at its joints, its limbs separated from one another, because the soul was not present in them to bind them together.
The soul, for its part, is bound in Hades, not with shackles, but with bonds.
Because of this, it could not help its own body to keep it from perishing in the earth.
For just as a pilot may die and his ship go down into the depths.
Likewise, if the soul were not bound in Hades, it would steer its body to keep it from decaying.
The soul, then, has been bound not only with chains, but also with its own sins, like ropes. Because of this it has become powerless and has left its body behind to decay in the earth.
The soul, meanwhile, is tormented in Hades, having become a footstool for death.
It remains in Hades, weeping and sighing over its beautiful body, saying:
“Where is my body, in which—in which—I used to sing hymns?
Where is my body, in which I used to pray to God?
Where is my beautiful body, in which I used to live as a human being among my friends and relatives, walking with them in it?
I used to dance in my body. For while I was in my body, they called me a human being. But now I am not a human being; I am a soul.
For when death separates the soul from the body, it is called a corpse, and it stinks.
I was looking for my body, not for my name, with which I used to be a human being and in which I used to speak.
For when the soul leaves its body, it no longer speaks in a beautiful voice, but in a constricted and very gloomy voice,
like a musical instrument that has no sound and is silent.
That is how the soul is when it does not have the body through which to cry out.
For it has decayed in the earth like a vessel that has broken and become useless. It has neither voice nor sound and is motionless, for it is a corpse.
For the soul that used to adorn it has gone away. The speaker has been taken away from it.
Indeed, it is impossible to recognize the appearance of anyone who has died, because he has shriveled in the sand.
You cannot recognize his face, the shape of his body, or his stature, nor do you hear anyone’s voice.
For a son will not recognize his own father, or his mother, or his brother, or his friend. It is impossible to recognize his face in the tombs.
His lips have shriveled, his skin has decayed, his eyes have closed, and the color of his face has changed. It is impossible to recognize any of them,
because all the bodies in the tombs have become alike. For they have decayed, and to us there is no distinction between them.
For we cannot identify a bone so that it can be joined to its own body, because the bone lies exposed, with no flesh covering it.
Even before the flesh covering the bone has decayed, you cannot recognize whose it is.
For who has ever identified a bone from among the limbs?
Or who can tell us the complexion of someone who has died?
For you cannot identify Adam’s bones, or which are those of the prophets, or which bodies are those of the patriarchs or the apostles.
They all lie scattered in the earth; their heads and their bodies lie scattered.
If a son looks for his father, he will not recognize him in the grave, nor will a friend recognize his friend, nor a brother his brother.
He will not find anyone’s name by which to recognize that it is really him, nor will he recognize his appearance, because they have turned to dust in the grave, with no human form left in them.
For humanity is scattered over the whole face of the earth and lies strewn everywhere. The earth is crowded with tombs and graves, and every place is filled with the stench of the dead.
The earth itself has become one single grave for the dead.
One human being was taken from the earth, but thousands upon thousands and tens of thousands upon tens of thousands have been buried in it.
Every place is filled with the dead: the sea and the rivers, the land and the mountains. Wild animals and birds have eaten their fill of the corpses of the dead.
And the underworld has been filled with souls in chains.
Oh, this creature formed from earth, so full of sorrow! Oh, this human creature, growing toward destruction and ending in sorrows and sighs!
The joy of those on earth lasts only an hour. They think it is great, but it quickly vanishes from their hands.
For here is someone rejoicing because he is going to marry a woman, and then he weeps over her when she has died.
Here is another rejoicing over his children, and then, look, he is weeping over their tomb.
Here is another delighting in his father, and afterward he mourns as his father is buried.
For what does a human being gain? A human being is sorrow with no comfort in it.
It is impossible to console someone who is going to perish, nor is there anyone who can comfort him.
He is a human being like him, and he too dies. How can a friend console his friend when he too is subject to death?
Or will a prophet of God comfort them? But they will not listen to him.
Indeed, they did not believe in the God of heaven, nor did they carry out his command, until they fell into death.
For he is still angry with humanity because of its transgression. The ways humanity perishes are beyond telling and description.
For everything oppresses human beings because of their transgression: sickness, loss, sorrow, grief, and the suffering that surrounds them;
cold and scorching heat, fire, wild animals, birds, reptiles, the seasons, and old age;
the winds and earthquakes, the rain and dew—all harm human beings.
The rivers drown them; they are devoured by wild animals, burned by fire, and destroyed by death.
They all despised humanity when it disobeyed God.
And when humanity was cast out of paradise, it came out onto this estate filled with suffering.
With envy, adultery, sexual immorality, and idolatry within it—for these are the things that caused humanity to die.
All these became death’s accomplices against humanity, and they armed themselves against humanity with lawless deeds so that death might destroy it.
For a human being never has any enjoyment at any time.
For when has a human being ever rejoiced?
Did he rejoice while he was in his mother’s womb?
How could he rejoice, packed into darkness and its stench, squeezed and cramped on every side in menstrual blood?
But did he rejoice as he came out of the womb?
For he was in even greater danger of dying.
But did he rejoice while he was in his mother’s lap
and nursing? Why does he cry out and weep?
For someone who is comfortable neither cries out nor weeps.
But did he rejoice when he was a little child crawling on the ground?
How could he rejoice when he was liable to have an animal come upon him and strike him dead, and his mouth was full of dust and dirt from crawling on the ground?
But if he becomes a young man, will he rejoice?
How will he rejoice?
He will not be able to rejoice.
For the ranks of youth surround him on every side with desires full of danger, and it is not good for him to act on them, lest he die miserably.
But when he takes a wife and has children, will he rejoice?
How will he rejoice when he is worried about his children, lest they go astray?
But if he grows old, how has he found relief?
Will he find relief when the dangers of old age are there?
And at the end of all these things is the expectation of death, which eats away at the soul like fire.
O death, which takes people of every age—children and the elderly, young people and adults!
For no age limit is set for death; rather, it takes people of every age. For what is human existence like?
For it is a great sorrow to look upon a person’s death and decay.
The face grows pale with the appearance of death, the body has grown cold, the mouth is shut, the hair has become matted, the eyes have grown dim and closed, and the limbs do not move.
For the remainder of the body in the earth—the flesh that has decayed, and the muscles that have become rags—
and the rest that has been stripped away, the joints that have come apart, the bones that have dried out, and the great quantity of dust—
for a human being is nothing, like a flower of the grass that dries up and decays, like wood that is burned by fire and consumed.
For after the destruction of the human being and his great misery,
God himself looked after his own creation, which he had made in his likeness and image, so that death would not be victorious
and boast, “I have conquered the human being.”
For the devil is always at war with humanity, and he took the human being captive through the evil of death and the gates of Hades,
constantly hurling his lawless deeds at him until he secured him under death’s power and shut him inside the prison of Hades.
Because of this, the soul, bound in darkness, could not free itself from the places where the dead are confined.
Because of this, the Father sent his Son to the earth without flesh, because he is a holy spirit.
He caused him to become flesh in the womb of the virgin, and God became human,
to save the one who was lost and gather those scattered through the devil’s envy, bringing them together into his flock.
Those whom death had scattered when it divided the human being, Christ gathered together, making the human being one again, soul and body.
For death bound the soul in Hades and dissolved the flesh in the earth, dividing the human being in two.
But the Savior Jesus freed the soul from its bonds and bound the flesh together again at its joints.
He brought the two together and made them one—the soul and the body—joining them to each other.
He gave the body to the soul, and the soul to the body.
He gave the instrument to the speaker; he gave him the limbs arranged in order.
Now then, O soul, sing in their body, since they have their own God, who is indestructible.
For this is why Christ died for us: so that we might live with him forever.
For did he owe a death that he had to die?
Or what need was there for him to become human?
Or did he himself need to take on flesh?
He is God, clothed in all the glory of divinity.
For this reason he endured being born as mortal human beings are, although he himself alone is the immortal God.
But why did he come down to earth, when he is the king who reigns over the heavens?
Who compelled him to offer his back to the cross and die joyfully?
He is the creator of everything, yet he endured being born from a woman's womb and being wrapped in swaddling clothes.
He who is clothed in all the glory of his Father.
He who sits upon the chariots of the cherubim was laid in a manger and suckled at a woman's breast.
He before whom seraphim stand trembling, glorifying his divinity.
He who sends rain to flow in the rivers, and sends floods and dew from heaven, was baptized in the Jordan by a mortal man.
He through whom everything receives light was humiliated by the Jews.
He at whose word the seven heavens, the firmament, the earth, and the underworld hang suspended was hung on a wooden cross.
He who took lifeless earth and shaped it into a living human being endured humiliation so that, through his humiliation, he might save the human being who had gone to destruction through his sin.
He gave his soul as a ransom for the souls of human beings.
He gave his holy flesh for the whole of Adam's created being, and he gave his blood for everyone.
He gave a human being for a human being, and his death for our death.
For death, which human beings owe and which they fear, has become a blessing because Christ died for us.
This is the love that Christ revealed when he died for us sinners so that he might save us.
For what righteous person has ever died for even one sinner?
Or what father has died for his own son whom he fathered?
Again, what friend has died for his friend?
Or a beloved brother for his brother?
For no one has ever done this: one person dying for another willingly or of his own accord.
But Christ himself came of his own accord, willingly and out of love.
We are sinners. Not only did he form us like Adam, making us human beings,
but when we were ruined by sin, he came and suffered for us, and in his love he brought us to life.
For when he formed us with his hand, he did not suffer. But now he has given birth to us again through the suffering of his death, suffering anguish for us like a woman in labor.
For he was exceedingly patient with us and did not burn up the world when he was being humiliated with whips at the hands of sinners.
He allowed them to kill him and bury him, just as the prophet says: “You have brought me down into the dust of death.”
Who seized him?
It was the ungodly people whom he loved, and they killed him.
He came to them to save them, and they spat him out like spit.
Look, then, O man, at the insults the children of Israel inflicted on our Lord.
They pierced the side of the one who created them.
They tormented the one who had done many good things for them and their ancestors.
They repaid good deeds with evil deeds, and the love with which he loved them with hatred.
They afflicted the one who had given them joy.
The one who raised the dead among them while they watched him.
The one who healed the lame and cleansed those with leprosy.
The one who gave light to the blind—they killed him and crucified him on a tree.
Look, then, O people, at the audacity of the Jews.
They hung up the one who suspended the earth.
They nailed up the one who established the world upon the waters of the rivers.
They tore apart the one who established the heavens in his wisdom.
They bound the one who freed them from slavery to Pharaoh.
They bound the one who releases sinners.
The one who gave them a spring of water and quenched their thirst—they gave him sour vinegar to drink.
And they fed him gall while he was in the agony of death on the cross, without remembering that he had given them honey to drink from a rock.
They bound the hands and feet of the one who released those who were imprisoned, held captive by the devil because they had done his will.
He kept them bound under his control until the one who would redeem those in captivity came and released those who were bound.
The one who sends the sun and moon to shine on them, who opened the eyes of the man blind from birth—they blindfolded him like a thief.
They buried the one who raised the dead.
Oh, this new and incomprehensible mystery!
They judged the judge.
They bound the one who forgives their sins.
They drove nails into the hands of the one who formed them.
They spat on the one who breathed their breath into their nostrils.
They split open the one who will split apart the limbs of their body.
[?] The one who watered the earth with life—they forced him to consume bitterness.
The one through whom everything lives died. For they did not insult him only on the cross; even before he died, they hurled great insults at him.
Then, while our Lord was hanging on the wood of the cross, the tombs opened and Hades split apart.
He rescued the souls and raised the dead. Many of the saints appeared in Jerusalem.
And the mystery had not yet been completed on the cross.
For when Christ died, he crushed the enemy. He bound the mighty tyrant. He set up his cross, [?] before them, bearing victory.
For our Lord Jesus Christ raised his body on the cross, and when Death saw Life, he fell beneath his feet.
Then the powers of heaven marveled at his wisdom.
The angels were astonished at him.
The elements were afraid, and all creation was shaken when they saw this new mystery and this terrifying sight.
They saw God hanging at the hands of human beings, who held him up on a piece of wood.
His feet were fastened to it with nails.
Likewise, his hands were stretched out, nailed to the wood.
The Jews, for their part, were mocking him, laughing and jeering. But they did not understand the mystery.
The earth trembled when it saw the shamelessness of the Jews.
The mountains and [?] hills were shaken and moved.
The sea raised its waves so as to cover the world.
The deep was shaken and opened its mouth to swallow them all.
Creation was shaken with anger at the filthy audacity of the Jews.
The lights of heaven grew dark. The sun set. The moon was shaken and hid itself. The stars ceased shining so that they would not give light to the ungodly.
The moon was full of light, yet it was not shining. So when the sun set, they were all in darkness.
They saw their God, who had created them, hanging on a tree like a robber.
The day became dark.
An angry angel came out from among all the angels, with his sword drawn in his hand, intent on wiping them out, ten thousand times ten thousand at once.
And when they were restrained by the mercy of Christ,
he reached for the curtain of the temple and tore it in two from top to bottom.
All the angels were looking out from heaven in anger, but the patience of God the Father restrained them all from destroying them.
The daylight fled and left the world in darkness—a thick darkness.
All these things happened before Christ closed his eyes.
And his light hurried forth and shone in Hades.
Hades trembled when the Lord descended into it, not in the flesh but in the spirit.
For he held everything together, because it was perishing before its time.
He poured his blood onto the earth, and it protected the earth and everything in it.
His body remained hanging on the tree because of the elements, while his spirit descended into Hades and saved those who were there.
He plundered Hades and took control of everything.
His body raised the dead on earth, while his spirit freed the souls in Hades.
For at the time when our Lord’s body was hanging on the cross, at that very time the tombs opened.
The gatekeepers of Hades saw him, trembled, and fled.
He shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars, and he brought their souls up from Hades to his Father.
For when the Lord overthrew Hades and trampled on death, he made a mockery of the enemy.
He brought the souls up from Hades, and he raised the bodies out of the earth.
Look, then, at the wondrous strength of his humanity as he hung dead on the tree.
For creation could not bear his dead body, nor could the elements bear him.
For Hades could not bear his spirit.
For every place was filled with turmoil over the sufferings of our Savior.
And all creation trembled at his death, for they could not endure seeing their Lord being despised.
All creation was torn apart, saying, “What is this new mystery?”
The Judge is being judged, and he does not speak.
They look at the one who cannot be seen, and they feel no shame.
They seize the one who cannot be seized, and he does not resist them.
They despise the one whom no one can equal, and he does not become angry.
The one who cannot suffer is suffering, and he does not become indignant.
The one who cannot die has died, and he has endured it.
They have buried in the earth the one who dwells in heaven, and he remains silent.
“What is this mystery?” said all creation, for they were all amazed at his acts of mercy.
And when he rose from the dead early on Sunday, when he trampled upon death,
he bound the tyrant and set humanity free.
Then all creation understood that the Judge had been judged for humanity’s salvation, and that for humanity’s sake they had seen the invisible one.
They measured the immeasurable one. The one who cannot suffer suffered. The one who cannot die died. They buried the one who belongs to heaven.
For they judged him as a human being [?], so that he might have mercy on us.
They killed him so that he might release those who were bound.
He suffered so that he might give us rest.
He died so that he might give us life.
They buried him so that he might raise us up.
If the Lord had not suffered in his humanity, how could humanity have been saved?
Then death fell beneath Christ’s feet, and he dragged it away as a trembling captive. Hades, with its power, turned back,
when it heard the Lord’s voice calling to all the souls, “Come out, you who are bound!
You who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, the light has risen upon you.
I proclaim life to you, for I am the Christ, the Son of God.”
Then he released the souls of the holy ones and raised them with him.
The earth, too, cried out, saying, “Spare me, Lord, and free me from the curse upon me. Remove the devil’s wickedness from me,
for you have made me worthy to have your body buried within me, in place of the blood that was poured out upon me, so that you might raise them up.
For your honored image has been scattered everywhere.
Yet if you had merely spoken the word, no one could have opposed your command. But your love compels you to come to what you have fashioned.
For look, you have taken your stand upon the earth, searching for the members of the being you fashioned.
Take man to yourself as a trust.
Take to yourself your image, which you entrusted to me.
Take Adam to yourself, unharmed, just as he was.
Then Christ rose from the dead on the third day and took the saints up with him to his Father.
For all humanity will be saved because of Christ’s death.
For it was one person whom they condemned, and the whole world was saved, and mercy was shown to the whole world.
Again, it was one person who died so that all might rise.
And the Lord died for everyone so that everyone would rise with him.
For when he died, he clothed himself with man and took him up with him to the heaven of heavens, united as one with him.
He took him as a gift to his Father.
It is not gold or silver, but man, whom he created according to his likeness and his image.
This, then, is the one whom the Father exalted.
He seated him at his right hand upon the lofty throne and appointed him judge of the living and the dead, and commander of his entire creation.
He is seated upon the cherubim, he who created the heavenly Jerusalem, who is the true bridegroom and the king of all ages.
Glory to him through all ages of ages. Amen.
Athanasius, Archbishop.
